title: Sandals on the throne
hookLine: an empty throne, and a pair of sandals keeping it
carry: the padukas: serving in the beloved's name
tomorrow: Ravana's own brother walks into Rama's camp. what does Rama do?

cards: A family might keep a seat empty at the table while someone's away. On the throne of Ayodhya there's no king. There's a pair of wooden sandals.
The man who could sit there lives outside the city in bark clothes, and every decision he makes, he makes in the sandals' name. His name is Bharata, and the sandals are his brother's.

teach.b: Bharata was given the kingdom by a promise his father made to Bharata's mother, the same promise that sent Rama into the forest. He wants none of it. In Valmiki's Ramayana he goes after Rama and begs him to come home.
Rama won't; his father's word stands.
So Bharata asks for his sandals, sets them on the throne, and rules as their servant.
In the Bhagavata, when Rama returns, Bharata comes out carrying the sandals on his head and sets them at his brother's feet.
That's why Hindus honor padukas, the sandals of God or a guru: the feet are where devotion bows. Now the week, in one breath. Bali offered himself, bhakti's last way.
Two bowls swapped, and svadharma followed a nature. One son obeyed, two refused: dharma is subtle. A father said kshama is strength.
The axe stepped aside, and the parampara went on. God came down as Rama to show us how. And here, a brother held a throne in someone else's name.

teach.h: LETTING GO OF WHAT YOU COULD KEEP.
teach.b: Different forms, different books, and in each, someone lets go of what they could have kept.

how: Bharata's devotion is told in Ramayana recitations and Ram Lila plays, and the image of the sandals, the padukas, is honored in Hindu worship as a sign of the one who wore them.

o: the brother who ruled in a pair of sandals' name
the city where Bharata waited outside the gates
the prince of Ayodhya, whose brother kept his place

games.q: the week, in pairs — tap them.
p: the third stride on a bowed head
ruled in his brother's sandals' name

s: Bharata plotted to get Rama sent away
the promise was made to his mother; Bharata wanted none of it.
Bharata begs Rama to come home and rule
Rama refuses, because his father's word stands.
Bharata takes the throne and rules as king
he sets Rama's sandals on it and rules as their servant.

games.q: at a friend's house you see a small pair of silver sandals on the family shrine. your friend isn't sure why they're there. what do you say?
o: they're padukas: like Bharata's, they stand for the one you serve, and you bow at the feet.
they're lucky charms for safe travel.
they're there to remind you to take your shoes off.
games.why: Bharata ruled as the sandals' servant and set them at Rama's feet when he came home. Hindus still honor padukas as the place devotion bows.

practice: Feel your feet on the floor, the soles resting, your weight settling down through them. Stay with that contact for the sit, steady and unhurried, as if someone else were keeping your place for you while you rest.

wordCard.voice: Rama: the prince whose brother set his sandals on the throne and ruled in their name until he came home.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sandals. Bharata's padukas, set on the throne, are honored in Hindu worship.

carryVoice: Your line: the padukas, serving in the beloved's name. Bharata kept the throne with a pair of sandals. A week ends here.
